title: Spark pursues a two-sided mandate: drive USDS adoption and deploy USDS collateral at risk-adjusted returns
content:
A.6.1.1.1.1 defines Spark as "an Agent focused on building on USDS in the Ethereum and adjacent DeFi ecosystem," and then states the mandate as two things at once: "driving adoption of USDS **and** deploying collateral backing USDS at attractive risk-adjusted returns."

These are not the same job. Driving adoption is a distribution and liquidity problem — get USDS into markets where people will hold and use it. Deploying collateral at attractive risk-adjusted returns is an asset-management problem — earn yield on the reserves that back the stablecoin. An Agent charged with only the first would grow a liability base with no earnings; one charged with only the second would be a fund with no reason to exist inside a stablecoin ecosystem.

The three-product structure follows directly from the double mandate: the Spark Liquidity Layer places liquidity, SparkLend creates borrow demand, and Spark Savings creates holding demand — while the collateral deployed across all three is what generates the return.

The load-bearing consequence is that Spark's performance cannot be judged on a single metric. Growth in USDS supply achieved by deploying collateral into poor risk-adjusted positions satisfies half the mandate while violating the other, and the Artifact's later operational parameters exist precisely to bound that trade-off.
description: The Agent is defined by both a demand-side and an asset-side objective simultaneously, which is why it needs three distinct products rather than one.
